<reason>Both sides argued with discipline and no fabricated evidence, but B did the more effective work of narrowing the debate to a concrete, decision-relevant tradeoff: opportunity cost of scarce, non-fungible resources versus the signaling value of a "standing floor." Critically, in the Pressure Questions exchange A was forced to define its floor's suspension threshold as an "equivalent existential threat" (Article 5-level), and B exploited this cleanly in Rebuttal 2 and the closing, showing that this threshold "discounts prevention" — a competing ally's defensive need could be highly valuable to address yet never qualify for reallocation under A's own definition. A never repaired this specific damage in its closing, instead pivoting back to its signaling argument. A's strongest move — quoting B's concession that "these signals cannot eliminate uncertainty" as fatal — was answered adequately by B's closing point that no policy eliminates uncertainty, symmetrizing rather than losing that exchange. B also sustained its treaty/nonmember distinction and procurement-without-recipient-designation counter-model without being dismantled. The result is that B left fewer live, unanswered burdens on the table at the end, giving it the cleaner path to victory, though the margin is not large because A's deterrence and alliance-cohesion logic remained forceful and rhetorically sharp throughout.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's exploitation of A's self-defined "equivalent existential threat" threshold (from A4.1) in B4.6-B4.8 and again in the closing (B5.2), showing that this threshold discounts legitimate preventive reallocation — a point A never squarely answered in its closing.</best_rebuttal>
